first_remarks.remarks_to_the_author:
This is a very interesting paper where authors curated a large dataset of head CT and radiology reports pairs and trained a model to perform report generation. This represents a valuable contribution given that only a few studies to date have been published on 3D scan report generation.

There are a few issues I'd like to note:

- 1) The evaluation metric the authors develop, FORTE, seems to be sound. However, it is hard to understand what these score mean in terms of quality; and to know whether they would align with medical experts evaluation.

I believe there are a few potential solutions here: a) performing a clinical content evaluation by medical experts and validating the alignment of the FORTE metrics with them. b) performing LLM-based evaluation. Many studies have shown good performance of LLMs at evaluating report generation tasks: FineRadScore (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20613), DocLens (https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09581), cheXprompt (https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08002) and RadFact

(https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04449).

Both of these approaches would add strength to the study, by providing a clear understanding of how well the report generation model performs.

- 2) I believe the "Turing test" described is more useful to understand the ability of the model to capture stylistic features of the outputs, but it's not strong as a clinical accuracy evaluation. Making the evaluators choose before showing the actual head CT scan may bias the final responses even after presenting the scan. A more robust evaluation of the reports would be to show both reports and the scans from the beginning.
- 3) How was the sentence pairing validated to ensure the pairing made sense?
- 4) There are many reports that only have pertinent negatives. How does negation removal affect the outputs of those reports?

## Minor comments:

- 5) While code was provided; it was not possible to run the code in the provided platform as it has limited resources. I believe there are also a few missing configuration files to run the code properly (e.g. RADICALchecked.json). The addition of documentation of data input format for the images, and a script for the evaluation pipeline would be helpful.
- 6) There are a few linguistic issues to immprove: for example, it's unclear what authors mean by 'pathologic features in complex neurovascular anatomies: i.e., the brain, the heart, the eye' and by 'impressions of neuronal and vascular features'. 'BrainGPT is trained on degeneration-oriented data and thus it fails to caption the malignancy tumor and acute traumatic features...'

It would be helpful for authors to provide more documented code, with clear instructions on how to run the model on the external dataset CQ500 to reproduce the results.

Recent studies such as LLaVA-Med and Med-PaLM M demonstrated the capability of interpreting and generating recommendations for X-ray and CT images. However, these models limited themselves in 2D images, and is not able to understand 3D medical imaging. In this work, the authors collected 18,885 text-scan pairs 3D-BrainCT dataset to fine-tune Otter model, and introduced four 'BrainGPT' models with their CVIT concept. Then, this work performed various of quantitative analysis to show its ability across different datasets. Additionally, this work invited 11 evaluators to evaluate whether the model generated caption is distinguishable or not compared to human-written captions. There are some strengths of this manuscript, including:

1. The curation of a large-scale 3D-BrainCT dataset with 18,885 text-scan pairs provides a valuable resource for training and evaluating models in this domain.
2. The proposed clinical visual instruction tuning (CVIT) approach effectively incorporates domain knowledge into the finetuning process, leading to improved model performance.
3. The introduction of the Feature-Oriented Radiology Task Evaluation (FORTE) metric addresses the limitations of traditional metrics and provides a more clinically relevant assessment of generated reports.
4. The impressive performance of BrainGPT on the external CQ500 dataset and the Turing test with physician evaluators demonstrates the model's potential for real-world application.
5. In short, this paper fine-tuned Otter model with their own dataset, followed by an extensive analysis of multiple experiments.

Overall I believe this is a solid and comprehensive work with many implications, however, it would be really helpful if the authors can further articulate the problems and results in a more clear manner.

My first concern is that the figure numbers do not go with the flow thus making this manuscript a bit difficult to follow. And I believe many of the figures do not clearly present the findings and the captions are not self-contained, making the audience difficult to read. For example, in Figure 6, the color on stacked bar chart was not described with legends. I have to check the main text to understand that red color means incorrect identification, whereas blue color means correct identification. However, this should better be directly indicated on the figure and caption. Also, explain 'before' and 'after' directly on Figure 6 caption. (This lack of information issue is not only exist in Figure 6, but also exist on other figures) Another example is Extended Data Fig. 2. It appears in both the introduction and discussion sections, but was not adequately addressed in the main Result section.

Additionally, based on the context and the title of this manuscript, I believe the manuscript is focusing on a 'holistic framework', which is the 'FORTE'. However, I believe the rationale of proposing 'FORTE' framework should be discussed in more detail (right now is less emphasized in the paper), especially how does it present as a critical challenge in both methodology perspective and the potential clinical adoption perspective. The current rationale 'Due to the potential instability caused by keyword frequency variance in report evaluations' is too practical and has limited additional implications.

Regarding the framework, I like the points that the efforts should be made to build a better evaluation metrics other than BLEU and METEOR in medical image report generation tasks. FORTE is a solid step towards this direction. Manually categorizing radiology keywords into degree, landmark, feature, and impression is based on the assumption that the report is highly unstructured. I hope every sentence in the report can contain one of those four elements but it is not the case. The author can provide a statistic to prove their points that on their dataset, the percentage of sentences contains four elements after "Negation Removal".

On the methodology side, this work fine-tuned Otter and named it 'BrainGPT', with subsequent experiments conducted by comparing the vanilla Otter to different versions of BrainGPT. However, I am unsure if the '3D' aspect is accurately defined, as it seems the system inputs multiple brain CT slices into the CLIP ViT large model and concatenates them in hidden space (embedding level) before incorporating them into the language model via cross attention. Since the convolution is not a real '3D', how does the model able to learn the relationship between each slice? It would be helpful to elucidate the model architecture, especially how the vision component is implemented, in the Methods section. Also, it would be helpful for the authors to discuss how this approach set itself apart from LLaVA-Med, Med-Flamingo, MiniGPT4, InstructBLIP, BLIP2, etc. (Since Otter is also based on Flamingo). Compared to Flamingo architecture, LLaVA-NeXT can also input multiple images. Therefore, can the author give some opinion on the rationale of choosing flamingo-style Otter over blip-2 style / LLaVA style MLLMs as a starting point?

Lastly, it would be beneficial to include a discussion on the potential limitations and biases of the 3D-BrainCT dataset, such as the demographic diversity and the prevalence of different pathologies.

## Others:

1. In abstract, 'Statistically, our BrainGPT model ……': the term 'statistically' may better be replaced by 'As a result', since 'statistically' usually stands for statistical analysis and significant observation.
2. Possible typo: In Main section, first paragraph: 'OpenI'.
3. Figures should be numbered according to the order in which they appear.
4. Figure 3: I recommend using a different color palette to highlight the vanilla Otter model.
5. Figure 4d: Indicate the statistical method that was used to derive the P-values, as well as whether it is one-side or twoside.
6. In this manuscript, 'negation removal' has not been described in methods. Therefore, I am a bit confused how 'negation removal' was conducted.
7. The fine-tuning process (CVIT with keywords instruction) and the evaluation metric (FORTE) are specifically designed for brain CT reports, which may limit the generalizability to other medical imaging modalities or anatomical regions. For every task (not even every target modality. for example, like abdominal CT contains multiple organ, each organ will needs a
8. "Extend Data Table 7"-like Degree-Landmark-Feature-Impression pair), FORTE keyword categories and list needs to be redesigned with a lot of manual labor. It would be great if the author can address this part.
8. Some artworks in Fig. 1, such as a hand with a feather pen, are likely GPT-generated. Suggest replace GPT-generated art with other royalty free arts.

(Remarks on code availability)

After a quick check of the code, all model checkpoints are available in Google Drive. Suggest hosting it on Huggingface.

unsorted.remarks_to_the_author:
The authors have provided revisions to their work that have clarified some issues but are still not satisfactory.

In particular, I have the following concerns:

- 1) I believe it is still not possible to determine, based on the information present in the manuscript, how clinically accurate is this model. The authors have provided on the rebuttal letter concordance metrics between FORTE and clinicians rating of paired sentences, which is relatively low (<0.40), even if better than other metrics. Therefore, even if we can probably agree on the fact that this model is better than others, or that the interventions they implemented on the base model improves its performance, I am still lacking an understanding of just how good the model really is, and how much work ahead there is to make this something usable. I strongly believe that either a formal clinical accuracy evaluation by experts, or an LLM-as-ajudge evaluation using one of the established LLM-based metrics would strengthen this by telling us how many clinically significant errors one can expect on these generated reports.
- 2) The sentence pairing has not been well validated to my understanding and I do not fully understand the benefit of it. The authors have provided a figure showing sentence pairing in one example; and even this example contains mismatches in sentences paired. In their figure, Ground Truth sentence D mentions the subudural hematoma, but it is matched with sentence F in the generated report, when it should be matched with B or H. Additionally, is sentence pairing only applied at the evaluation step (as it needs the ground truth report) to re-order reports and increase the traditional generation metrics? As a clinician, I care much less about the traditional natural language metrics than clinical accuracy metrics.

(Remarks on code availability)

I appreciate the authors' responses, especially regarding the modeling aspect - including the 3D component. The explanation of learnable positional encoding clarified my understanding, and I agree with the authors' statements on this "3D" learning. The authors have fully addressed all my concerns.

(Remarks on code availability) The code is complete.

3. > Respond : We thank the reviewers for their insightful questions. To establish an evaluation metric and to prove the validity of the metric itself was a specialized sector that required well designed experiments to aggregate confident results for the general researchers in the medical informatic domain.

In this manuscript, starting from the inadequacy of the traditional language metrics in medical report evaluation, we postulated that the general semantic architecture (lesion feature + degree + landmark = impression ) of a common radiology description could form a evaluation system that possess a better fitness to weight the medical relevance of a generated report. On top of the original included tests, we asked 2 physicians to detail evaluate the descriptive and diagnostic content of the generated report, then correlate the physician rated score either with the FORTE score or the traditional LLM metrics. The detail was unfolded as follow:

- -Regarding the expert evaluation, we constructed a physician survey including 60 random samples from the lowest and highest one-third sentence pairs (30 sentence

pairs each) with regard to the average FORTE score. The physicians are then asked to answer two 5-scale likert scores in descriptive and diagnostic features. Since the objective (traditional metrics and FORTE scores) and subjective scores (physician survey) are continuous and discrete variables respectively, we transformed the objective scores into the same scale as the subjective scores (fig. a). Then, we computed Cohen's kappa coefficient for inter-rater agreement as metrics of concordance. The results (fig. b) showed that FORTE (0.10-0.35) achieves twice higher alignment with physician survey than traditional metrics (0.00-0.17). Moreover, the concordance between the average FORTE score and physician raters was the highest (0.24-0.39). The results indicate that the FORTE score is a more clinically precise (higher concordance with medical providers), explainable (in descriptive and diagnostic aspect), and generalizable (considering the terms of degree, landmark, feature, and impression) metric.

Indeed, these studies all proposed solid evaluation methods, and they all shared a common viewpoint that traditional evaluation methods such as BLEU and ROUGE fail to gauge complex radiology reports. To this end, FORTE, as a comprehensive framework that performs sentence-pairing, negation removal, and 4-categories keyword extraction, serves as a hallucination-free and interpretable convergence that can be easily understood by healthcare providers.

> Respond: Dear reviewer, we think this comment is a very interesting perspective. We both agreed that the completeness of an AI generated radiology report should encompass the (1) semantic (2) accuracy (3) and style of the diagnostic content. Therefore, we kindly unpacked this question in different segments of our experiment, which is elucidated in the re-illustrated Fig.1. Originally, the semantic aspects were evaluated in Fig. 4 (established and curated in FORTE experiments), the accuracy of the captioned report was validated from an external

Thus, the remaining un-approached component of the radiology report was the stylistic quality, for which the Turing test (Fig. 6) may be an optimal experiment design. This section is inspired from the origin design of the Turing test, which involved a human raised query (in our case: asked for a brain CT caption), and returned with a contextual report, wherein the image context was not involved.

## Reviewer: (3) How was the sentence pairing validated to ensure the pairing made sense?

> Respond: We fully agree with the reviewer that the sentence pairing is a crucial step in the FORTE framework. Over the past few decades, measuring semantic similarity has played a critical role in natural language processing. We follow BERTScore (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.09675), which leverages contextual embeddings and cosine similarity to achieve better semantic matching than traditional n-gram-based methods. Previous literature showed the BERT embeddings (https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805) capture rich semantic information and are widely recognized as effective for sentence similarity tasks. (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.01852, https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.05864, https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.00512) Cosine similarity, which measures the token-level contextual embeddings of reference and candidate sentences, is widely recognized as an effective generation metric and applied in the CheXbert vector similarity metric. (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2023.100802) Although the pairing is automated, the user can validate the quality of the pairings by calculating traditional metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, or METEOR for the paired sentences and showing that they yield similar or better scores compared to an unpaired baseline. In Fig. 3b, we showcased that the traditional metric scores for every BrainGPT model were significantly improved (p < 0.001). In this regard, the sentence pairing method is a valid method that adapts the traditional metrics to the detailed, itemized, and differential diagnosis-oriented format of brain CT reports.

In addition, we compared our method with the BLEU score as the standard for sentence pairing. For baseline Otter-generated reports, the concordance rate is only 30.99%, while for BrainGPT-generated reports, the concordance rate is 57.99% (BrainGPT-plain), 60.22% (BrainGPT-example), 62.33% (BrainGPT-template), 62.30% (BrainGPT-keyword). This interesting positive correlation between report quality and sentence pairing concordance rate validated the stability of our method in high-quality radiology reports. In the following figure, we showcase the sentence pairing comparison between our method and BLEU score for the example in Fig. 1. Although different in two pairs, the mismatched content (lacunar infarction/ no remarkable finding in sinuses and mastoids) is not relevant to the main impression (subdural hemorrhage).

Reviewer: (4) There are many reports that only have pertinent negatives. How does negation removal affect the outputs of those reports?

<!-- image -->

> Respond: Dear reviewer, this is a constructive question that encouraged us to underline some noteworthy findings in our negation removal analysis.

While the radiologists may have a clinical-oriented description focus which only reports prioritized negation description, BrainGPT generates numerous minor important negation descriptions, which dilutes statistical caption efficacy. Therefore, we simply removed sentences with 'no' in order to confine the description range to only positive findings. Particularly, reports that only had pertinent negatives were usually describing healthy patients (BrainGPT-plain: 21.47% , BrainGPT-example: 24.83%, BrainGPT-template: 24.63%, BrainGPT-keyword: 26.21%).

> Respond: Dear reviewer, we think this comment is very critical in understanding the value of our study. Over the past few years, measuring imaging caption quality has been a critical topic in natural language processing, as it determines the way we evaluate model performance. Specifically, the advances in multi-modal capability of report generation studies emphasized the importance of medical text evaluation methods. In the initial introduction paragraph, we mentioned the advantage of the CheXpert classifier over traditional imaging evaluation metrics while pointing to the lack of comprehensiveness in addressing the multi-semantic context of CT reports. Later in the FORTE result paragraph, we further proposed a solid evaluation method that should deal with keyword frequency variance in the experiment inspired by the frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF). In the revised manuscript, we have rephrased this rationale to 'On the basis of the keyword frequency experiment and a thorough analysis of the CheXpert classifier, we consider that a clinically-sensible evaluation metric should encompass a structured keyword extraction concept that (1) addresses the multi-semantic context of radiology reports, (2) allows the recognition of synonyms to detect a broader array of related terms and (3) can be transferred across multiple modalities. In this regard, we introduced the feature-oriented radiology task evaluation (FORTE). This method gauges the medical content of the generated report by focusing on the density of radiology information. We categorized radiology keywords and their synonyms into degree, landmark, feature, and impression subsets to perform a multi-faceted evaluation of the system's performance. '

Since the other reviewer has also mentioned the importance of elucidating the rationale and clinical meaning for FORTE, we provide the comparison between FORTE and other novel methods including Doclens (2024/02/18), FineRadScore (2024/05/30), RadFact (2024/06/06) and CheXprompt (2024/06/27) in the discussion paragraph. (see re-illustrated Extended Data Table 7) These studies all shared a common viewpoint that traditional evaluation methods such as BLEU and ROUGE fail to gauge complex radiology reports. We found (1) similar to the sentence pairing process of FORTE, most of them adopt sentence-level comparison when prompting GPT to adapt to the list-by-list nature of radiology reports (2) in coherence with the issue raised in our negation removal session, Doclens mentioned the importance for the evaluation method to discriminate 'there is a focal lesion' from 'there is no focal lesion'(3) most importantly, ranging from sentence-level precision and recall to error counting, every study aims to establish a more clinically precise, explainable, and generalizable metric. To this end, FORTE, as a comprehensive framework that performs sentence-pairing, negation removal, and 4-categories keyword extraction, serves as a hallucination-free and interpretable convergence that can be easily understood by healthcare providers.

Despite the imperfection of our sentence pairing method, we deem the approach as a more economical and crash-resistant solution compared to LLM-based pairing. We agree with the reviewers that clinical accuracy metrics are of paramount importance, far surpassing  traditional  natural  language  metrics.  In  light  of  this,  we  have  designed  our framework, FORTE, to address the limitations of traditional language metrics and prioritize clinical relevance. The sentence pairing process is applied exclusively during the evaluation step to reorder the generated reports, thereby improving the accuracy of evaluation based on traditional  generation  metrics.  Furthermore,  we  performed  a  Pearson  correlation  analysis between DocLens and FORTE, with and without sentence pairing preprocessing. Interestingly, we found that all four FORTE categories, as well as the average FORTE F1 score, exhibited higher correlations with DocLens when sentence pairing was applied, underscoring the value of this approach.
